explanations: terra: The mindful spend from what God has provided them, turning rizq into circulation rather than treating it as a sealed personal stock.
terra: Twelve springs emerge, each group knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink from God's provision without corruption.
terra: Those who conceal revelation for a small price eat only fire into their bellies, a close parallel to orphan-property becoming fire in 4:10.

luna: Righteousness includes giving wealth, despite love for it, to kin, orphans, and the needy; the section's love of money is reversed into sharing it. | terra: Righteousness includes giving wealth عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ to kin, orphans, the needy, traveler, requester, and for liberation, reversing love of wealth into a shared table.

luna: The bequest for parents and near relatives at death shows another way a person's property is apportioned to those who follow, alongside the section's treatment of inheritance. | terra: When death approaches one who leaves wealth, a fair bequest for parents and near relatives is prescribed, directing the departing owner's store toward named claimants.
terra: فِدْيَةٌۭ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍۢ makes feeding a needy person the concrete compensatory act for one unable to fast.

luna: Do not consume one another's property wrongfully or use it to bribe authorities; its prohibition supplies the legal opposite of the section's image of consuming an estate wholesale. | terra: The command not to eat one another's wealth unjustly or use rulers to consume a portion of others' property gives the legal-social form of the section's predatory eating.

luna: Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, needy people, and travelers; it lays out recipients for the surplus that the section shows being swallowed. | terra: The answer to what should be spent names parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, directing wealth toward almost the same absent guests as the section's table.
terra: Asked what to spend, the answer is the surplus beyond need, identifying what should leave a vessel rather than accumulate in it.

luna: Asked about orphans, the reply is to improve their affairs and treat them as kin, warning that God distinguishes corrupters from reformers; it gives an ethical boundary for managing the property the section says is consumed. | terra: Concerning orphans, reform is best; if their property is mixed with the guardian's, they remain brothers, and God knows the corrupter from the reformer.
terra: The divorced woman receives a fair provision according to the wealthy or constrained giver's capacity, applying measure to a vulnerable person's material due.
terra: Divorced women are assigned a fair provision as a duty on the mindful, another named share that must leave an owner's wealth.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied many times, while God constricts and expands; true increase comes through giving within His measure.
terra: Spend from what God provided before a day without trade or rescuing friendship; apportioned provision has a time in which it can still be released.

luna: Spending wealth in God's way is compared to a grain that multiplies its yield; the source section's secondary dictionary form حبّ for grain meets its contrast between piled wealth and food given away. | terra: Spending wealth is pictured as one حَبَّةٍۢ growing seven ears of a hundred grains: the section's grain-sense of h-b-b leaves the hoard and becomes true increase through giving.

luna: Those who spend and do not follow their giving with reminders or injury receive their reward; this adds the section's distinct requirement that sharing the needy person's portion preserve their dignity.
luna: A good word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt; alongside the section's call to speak kindly at a distribution, this marks the boundary between helping and humiliating.
luna: This warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity, giving a specific contrary case to the section's meal and its instruction to treat recipients kindly.
terra: A garden heavy with fruit is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its aged owner has weak offspring, joining abundant food, vulnerable dependents, and consuming fire in one loss.

luna: The command is to spend good things from earnings and produce, not what the giver would only accept with closed eyes; it specifies the quality of the share offered to the needy. | terra: Spend from the good things earned and produced from earth, and do not select what is defective for others; the shared table must receive food the giver would accept.
luna: Satan threatens poverty and commands miserliness, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this identifies the fear of scarcity that can keep the section's needy person unfed.

luna: The verse says giving charity openly is good and concealing it for the poor is better; it develops the concrete act of transferring wealth to people in need. | terra: Open charity is good, but hidden charity given to the poor is better, keeping the needy person's receipt central while removing the giver's display.

luna: Poor people are described as restrained from traveling and not importuning others, though their need can be recognized; it adds the hidden, self-contained need behind the section's vulnerable guest. | terra: The restrained poor are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not ask insistently, showing that the needy person's absent request does not erase the share within the full vessel.
luna: Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, receive their reward; this neighboring statement offers the inverse social practice to the section's failure to encourage feeding.
terra: God destroys usurious increase and causes charities to grow, reversing the accumulator's account of what diminishes and what multiplies.
terra: The disbelievers' wealth and children will avail nothing, and they become وَقُودُ ٱلنَّارِ; stored assets fail while their owners become fuel.

luna: Accumulated gold, silver, animals, and crops are named among worldly desires; this gives concrete contents to the section's object of intense attachment to wealth. | terra: The love of desires is adorned, including heaped gold and silver; its قَنَٰطِيرِ ٱلْمُقَنطَرَةِ gives the section's intense love of wealth an explicitly piled material form.
terra: Mary receives provision in the sanctuary and identifies God as its source, who provides without account, a scene of sustenance arriving beyond ordinary control.
terra: Even مِلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًۭا, an earth-full quantity of gold, cannot ransom the one who dies rejecting faith, giving the full-container image its absolute limit.

luna: One cannot attain righteousness until spending what one loves; this turns the section's intense love of money into a test of willingness to give. | terra: لَن تَنَالُوا۟ ٱلْبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُوا۟ مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ makes spending precisely what one loves the road to goodness, rather than love's reason for retaining it.
luna: The righteous spend in both ease and hardship; this is a specific response to the section's measured changes in provision and its question of whether the needy are fed when others have plenty.

luna: Those who withhold God's bounty will have what they withheld around their necks, and the inheritance of heavens and earth belongs to God; this directly joins hoarded wealth to its eventual return. | terra: Those who clutch God's bounty will have it collared around them, while وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَٰثُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ denies that their hoard was ever finally theirs.
terra: The demanded sign is an offering consumed by fire, giving the section's cited dictionary sense of fire 'eating' something a direct Quranic scene.

luna: ولا تأكلوا أموالهم إلى أموالكم directly forbids adding orphans' property to one's own and consuming it, the very taking that the section's wording about eating inheritance exposes. | terra: The ban on eating orphan property by adding it إِلَىٰٓ أَمْوَٰلِكُمْ directly opposes the section's لَمًّا, which gathers distinguishable shares into one mass.

terra: Property is called the means God made قِيَٰمًۭا, and guardians must وَٱرْزُقُوهُمْ فِيهَا; this directly supports the section's claim that a vulnerable person's provision lets that person remain standing.

luna: Guardians must deliver orphans' property when they mature and must not consume it wastefully or hastily beforehand; this is a precise limit on taking the estate the section says is being eaten up. | terra: Guardians must hand orphans their property and not eat it wastefully or hastily before they grow, a precise procedural barrier against consuming the whole legacy.

luna: The source section calls sustenance a share and names the fixed portion of inheritance; this verse assigns a portion to both men and women from what relatives leave, including little or much, making the legal share explicit. | terra: نَصِيبًۭا مَّفْرُوضًۭا makes inheritance an obligatory apportioned share for women as well as men, the precise boundary erased when the legacy is eaten all together.

luna: At the division, relatives, orphans, and the needy who are present are to be given something from it and addressed kindly; this is the section's inheritance meal in a single scene. | terra: At the inheritance division (ٱلْقِسْمَةَ), relatives, orphans, and the needy are present and the command فَٱرْزُقُوهُم مِّنْهُ gives them provision from it, assembling the section's whole table in one act.
terra: Those dividing an estate must imagine leaving their own weak offspring behind and speak rightly, bringing the vulnerable child's future into the inheritance scene.

luna: This ayah says that those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire in their bellies; it makes literal the section's link between eating the vulnerable's wealth and the fire brought at judgment. | terra: Those who eat orphan wealth unjustly إِنَّمَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِى بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًۭا makes literal the section's meeting between devouring the weak person's property and the fire the eater finally meets.

luna: The inheritance shares here are measured by kinship and circumstance, concretely showing what it means for a passed estate to be divided among its rightful recipients. | terra: The prescribed shares for children and parents enact the separation of an inheritance into its owners' portions rather than allowing an undivided eater to seize it.

luna: This ayah gives specified portions to spouses and maternal siblings; it develops the source section's claim that inherited property passes in measured shares rather than being swallowed together. | terra: The spouses' and siblings' shares continue the measured inheritance table, repeatedly calling each allocation فَرِيضَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ.
terra: After the measured inheritance shares, obedience to those limits leads to gardens; this is the positive boundary around the division.
terra: Transgressing the inheritance limits leads to abiding fire, joining violation of apportioned shares to the section's fiery endpoint.

luna: The prohibition on inheriting women against their will and pressuring them to take back part of what was given marks coercive inheritance as the opposite boundary to a rightful share. | terra: The prohibition on inheriting women by compulsion exposes another abuse hidden under inheritance language: treating a vulnerable person herself as property to be seized.

luna: This ayah forbids consuming one another's wealth unjustly, except by mutual trade; it marks a general boundary against the unjust taking specified in the section's inheritance scene. | terra: لَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ generalizes the section's eating image to all wrongful appropriation of one another's property.

luna: Men and women each have a نصيب from what they earn, and the verse directs people to ask God for bounty; this connects the section's defined share to livelihood gained by different people. | terra: Men and women each have a share of what they earn, and envy is redirected into asking God from His bounty, preserving distinct portions under divine giving.

luna: The verse appoints heirs to what parents and close relatives leave and tells people to give each claimant their نصيب; this directly joins inheritance to assigned portions. | terra: The verse appoints heirs for what parents and relatives leave and commands that contracted associates be given their share, another explicit barrier against swallowing the estate whole.
terra: The command to worship God is immediately joined to good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, travelers, and dependents, laying out the social table around property.

luna: This condemns miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God's bounty; it names the community-wide refusal to share that the section distinguishes from a lone miser's act. | terra: The condemned are stingy, command other people to stinginess, and hide God's bounty; this is the communal reverse of urging one another toward feeding.

luna: The ruling invokes orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld and calls for justice toward orphan children; it makes the section's concern with the orphan's rightful portion specific to those denied it within family arrangements. | terra: The ruling concerns orphan women whose prescribed due is withheld and weak children, then commands justice for orphans; it directly exposes who is erased when inheritance is swallowed whole.

luna: The final inheritance ruling sets out a sibling's portion, another concrete boundary on who receives a share of an estate. | terra: The final inheritance ruling assigns the kalalah estate by stated fractions, reinforcing that a legacy passes by measured shares rather than indiscriminate gathering.
terra: The expiation feeds ten needy people from the average food used for one's own family, bringing the poor onto the same standard of table rather than assigning scraps.
terra: When warnings are forgotten, the doors of every thing are opened; at the moment of exultant fullness the recipients are seized and left despairing.
terra: God splits the grain and date-stone and brings life from death, supplying a direct Quranic use of the grain-sense of h-b-b developed by the section.
terra: Rain produces vegetation and clustered grain, locating the jar's imagined grain within a visible chain of divine provision.

luna: The verse describes pagans assigning portions of crops and livestock to God and their partners, then distorting the allocation; this is a concrete, contrary use of the section's language of apportioned livelihood. | terra: People assign God a share of crops and cattle, then let the partners' portion displace God's; the corrupt partition of provision exposes how a declared share can be redirected by power.

luna: After naming gardens, crops, and fruit as provision, the verse commands giving their due on harvest day and forbids excess; it directly joins food, a rightful share, and restraint. | terra: At harvest, وَءَاتُوا۟ حَقَّهُۥ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِۦ commands release of the crop's due and immediately forbids excess, joining grain, entitlement, and the boundary on filling oneself.

luna: This command forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity, alongside full measure and just weight; it connects protection of a vulnerable share with fair measure. | terra: Protection of orphan property stands in the same verse as full measure and weight with justice, joining the vulnerable owner to honest apportionment.
terra: لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ sets a decreed filling of Hell beside 50:30's still-demanding vessel; together they mark how different this fullness is from sufficiency.

luna: In Shuayb's address, people are told to give full measure and weight and not deprive others of their goods; it is a specific boundary against taking the portion owed to someone else. | terra: Shuayb's command combines full measure and weight, refusal to deprive people of their things, and refusal to corrupt the earth, the whole ethical boundary around the filled container.
terra: The oppressed people inherit the blessed eastern and western lands, reversing possession from oppressors to the formerly weak.
terra: The twelve tribes each know their spring while manna and quails are provided, a scene where water and food are apportioned to a whole community.
terra: True believers spend from divine provision, making release of the allotted share part of their response to God.

luna: The war-gain ruling assigns a fifth to named recipients and distributes the remainder in its legal setting; the source section explicitly gives ق س م the dictionary sense of dividing booty among its owners. | terra: The fifth of spoils is apportioned to God, the Messenger, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, directly realizing the dictionary sense of dividing booty among its proper recipients.
terra: Blood relatives are declared closer to one another in God's Book, establishing the kinship order within which inherited property is apportioned.

luna: The verse lists love of wealth among attachments preferred over God, His Messenger, and striving; it marks the boundary where attachment to possessions outranks duty. | terra: The verse gathers loved relatives, acquired wealth, feared commercial decline, and pleasing dwellings, then tests whether these are loved more than God and His cause.

luna: This condemns religious authorities who consume people's wealth wrongfully and hoard gold and silver without spending it; it is a close parallel to consuming inheritance while refusing the poor. | terra: Religious authorities يَأْكُلُونَ أَمْوَٰلَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ while others hoard gold and silver instead of spending, joining wrongful eating and the filled hoard in one verse.

luna: The next ayah shows that hoarded gold and silver heated and used to brand their owners; it completes the warning about stored wealth in 9:34. | terra: The hoard from 9:34 is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, sides, and backs, making stored wealth itself the fire with which its keepers meet.
terra: The Prophet is told not to admire their wealth and children, for God wills to punish them through those very possessions in worldly life.

luna: Alms are assigned to named recipients including the poor and needy, showing provision deliberately directed toward people absent from the wealthy table. | terra: Obligatory alms are expressly apportioned among the poor, needy, collectors, reconciliation, freeing people, debtors, God's way, and travelers, a divinely fixed counter-table to private accumulation.
terra: Hypocrites urge one another toward wrong, forbid right, and close their hands, a communal inverse of reciprocal urging toward the needy person's food.
terra: Earlier peoples had greater wealth and children and enjoyed their allotted share; the addressees likewise enjoy their share and plunge as they did, joining abundance, portion, and moral loss.
terra: Some covenant that if God gives them from His bounty they will give charity and become righteous, making promised sharing depend on received provision.
terra: When God gives them from His bounty they become stingy and turn away, staging the full vessel's closure at the moment it is filled.
terra: Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the day they meet God, giving retained bounty an inward consequence.
terra: The warning not to admire wealth and children is repeated, again turning apparent abundance into an instrument of punishment rather than honor.
terra: Every creature's provision rests with God, who knows its dwelling place and repository; the verse explicitly holds rizq, staying, and storage together.

luna: Shuayb again commands full measure and weight and forbids reducing people's due, repeating the measured-fairness boundary that illuminates the section's swallowed inheritance. | terra: Shuayb sees his people in prosperity yet fears punishment while forbidding deficient measure and weight, showing abundance does not authorize taking another's share.
terra: The command to fulfill measure and weight justly and not diminish people's goods directly regulates how a provisioned community portions its table.
terra: After the commands for honest measure, the remainder left by God is declared better than wrongful gain, reversing the fear that fairness empties one's vessel.
terra: لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ repeats the decree to fill Hell, sharpening the paradox of the vessel that in 50:30 asks for more.

luna: Joseph tells the people to cultivate grain for seven years and leave most of it in its ears; this is measured food storage in preparation for scarcity, unlike swallowing an inheritance all at once.
luna: The seven hard years consume what was stored, except a little kept back; the verse shows a reserve used by measured need rather than amassed for private excess.
luna: The famine plan ends with a year of rain and pressing, the return of abundance after rationing; it completes the passage's contrast between need and provision.
luna: Joseph asks to oversee the land's storehouses as a knowledgeable keeper; controlled reserves serve public need, a specific counterexample to the section's unshared accumulation.
luna: During famine Joseph distributes provisions to his brothers from the storehouses; it stages food allotment to people who have come in need.

luna: Joseph promises to give full measure and calls attention to that practice, an exact scene of food allotted by measure. | terra: Joseph says أَنَا۠ أُوفِى ٱلْكَيْلَ while distributing grain and conditions the visitors' next ration, staging provision as a full, governed measure.

luna: Joseph sets a condition on the next measure if his brother is not brought; the boundary shows provision being allocated by a stated rule rather than seized as one mass. | terra: Without the brother, فَلَا كَيْلَ لَكُمْ عِندِى: the measured share can be withheld entirely, showing the authority embedded in control of the granary.

luna: Joseph's brothers describe the harm touching their family and ask for full measure and charity; this is a hungry household asking for its ration and an additional act of giving. | terra: The distressed family brings scant merchandise and asks Joseph فَأَوْفِ لَنَا ٱلْكَيْلَ وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَآ, linking full measure with generosity to people in need.
luna: This says that all things are with God according to a measure, in a passage about what wombs carry and release; it extends the section's q-d-r claim beyond a person's visible portion of wealth.
terra: Those who spend from provision secretly and openly are placed among people seeking God's face, the opposite stance from hoarding for permanence.

luna: Allah expands provision for whom He wills and measures it down; this directly illustrates the section's link between رزق and measured allotment. | terra: ٱللَّهُ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ directly supplies the section's claim that provision is expanded or measured narrowly by God, while the verse relativizes worldly enjoyment.
terra: Believers must spend from provision secretly and openly before a day without trade or friendship, giving the allotted share a finite time for use.

luna: Abraham says he settled part of his descendants in an uncultivated valley and asks God to provide fruit for them; this concretely links the source section's derived س ك ن sense of the needy person's settledness to sustenance that lets a community remain. | terra: Abraham settles his offspring in an uncultivated valley and asks that they be provided with fruits; provision is what enables dwelling in the section's secondary s-k-n sense.

luna: The verse says provision treasures are with God and that He sends things down only in a known measure; it links stored abundance to measured distribution. | terra: Every thing has its treasuries with God, but He sends it down only بِقَدَرٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ, joining stored abundance to an exact released measure.
terra: God gives life and death and declares that He is the inheritor, a compact statement of the section's claim that all possession finally returns to the One who remains.
terra: They assign to unknown objects نَصِيبًۭا مِّمَّا رَزَقْنَٰهُمْ, joining provision and portion in a wrongful distribution for which they will be questioned.

luna: God has favored some over others in provision, yet the favored do not share it with those under their authority; this exposes the social refusal to redistribute the unequal shares the section describes. | terra: God has favored some in provision, yet the favored refuse to return their provision to those under their authority so that they might share equally; unequal rizq becomes a test of withheld sharing.
terra: The one granted good provision فَهُوَ يُنفِقُ مِنْهُ سِرًّۭا وَجَهْرًا spends from it secretly and openly, the opposite motion from filling and sealing the vessel.
terra: God makes houses a place of rest and provides portable dwellings, developing the s-k-n sense through the material means that let people remain somewhere.
terra: مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍۢ distinguishes the exhaustible contents people hold from what remains with God, exposing the false permanence of accumulation.
terra: A secure, settled town receives abundant provision from every place, then ingratitude turns that abundance into enveloping hunger and fear.

luna: The relative, poor person, and traveler are each to be given their due; this is a direct Qur'anic formulation of a portion reaching people beyond its owner. | terra: وَءَاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ commands delivery of the relative's due and the needy person's due, treating what leaves one's hand as their right.

luna: The hand is not to be chained to the neck or extended completely, lest a person end up blamed and destitute; it contrasts withholding with measured giving. | terra: Do not keep the hand chained to the neck or extend it without limit; the commanded middle regulates both hoarding and ruinous emptying.

luna: The same expansion and restriction of provision is attributed to the Lord who sees His servants; it shows that an individual's wealth is measured rather than proof of honor or humiliation. | terra: إِنَّ رَبَّكَ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ repeats the exact divine expansion and restriction that governs the section's idea of each person's measured share.

luna: The orphan's property may be approached only in the best way until the orphan reaches maturity, a direct boundary on the section's image of eating another's inheritance. | terra: Do not approach orphan property except in the best manner until maturity, a direct boundary around the vulnerable heir's share.

luna: The command is to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance; it supplies a concrete rule for respecting another person's measured due. | terra: أَوْفُوا۟ ٱلْكَيْلَ إِذَا كِلْتُمْ commands fullness in measuring for another and an upright balance, a just use of the brimful measure.

luna: If people possessed the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; it directly exposes the impulse to keep a stock rather than feed others. | terra: If humans possessed the treasures of God's mercy, they would still withhold for fear of spending; the verse diagnoses the impulse behind the sealed full vessel.

luna: The owner of two gardens boasts that he has more wealth and supporters than his companion, a concrete scene of possession used to rank people. | terra: The garden owner boasts أَنَا۠ أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًۭا and greater manpower, a narrative embodiment of rivalry in abundance.
terra: Entering his garden while wronging himself, he says it will never perish, joining fullness to the fantasy of permanence.

luna: The same owner doubts the Hour and assumes that if returned to his Lord he will find something better; this reveals the false afterlife confidence attached to his wealth. | terra: He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return, extending wealth's false promise beyond death.
terra: The poorer companion says the garden owner should have acknowledged God's will and power on entering, correcting the claim of self-secured abundance.

luna: The garden owner's wealth and harvest are ruined and he regrets associating partners with his Lord; this completes the neighboring warning that abundance cannot secure what he owns. | terra: When the fruit is destroyed, he turns his palms over what he spent while the garden lies ruined, the full estate abruptly emptied.
terra: No company can help him apart from God and he cannot help himself, exposing the social power attached to abundance as unusable.
terra: After the garden's collapse, true protection belongs to God and His reward and outcome are best, replacing the failed protection of wealth and followers.

luna: Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds remain; this gives the section's accumulated property a clear limit. | terra: Wealth and children are the adornment of the near life, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; the verse separates the filled vessel from what actually lasts.
terra: ٱسْتَطْعَمَآ أَهْلَهَا stages the dictionary form cited in the section: two travelers ask a town for food, and its people refuse them hospitality.

luna: The boat belongs to miskin people working at sea, and al-Khidr damages it to keep a king who seizes every sound boat from taking it; this reverses the section's powerful taking the vulnerable's property. | terra: The boat belongs to needy people who work at sea and faces confiscation by a king, showing that a miskin can possess productive property yet remain weak before power.

luna: A treasure is preserved for two orphans until they mature because their father was righteous; this reverses consuming an orphan's inheritance by showing property protected for its rightful young owners.

luna: The verse says God will inherit the earth and all upon it and that people will be returned to Him; it names the eventual return of property and owners in the source section. | terra: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَرِثُ ٱلْأَرْضَ وَمَنْ عَلَيْهَا states the final transfer: God remains, inherits earth and everyone on it, and all return to Him.
terra: Paradise is the garden God gives as inheritance to mindful servants, an inheritance received from divine promise rather than taken from the weak.
terra: A rejecter claims he will surely be given wealth and children, carrying the assumption that possession is a continuing personal entitlement.
terra: وَنَرِثُهُۥ مَا يَقُولُ strips that claimant of the wealth he names and makes God its inheritor while he comes alone.
terra: Do not stretch the eyes toward worldly splendor used as a test; the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
terra: لَا نَسْـَٔلُكَ رِزْقًۭا نَّحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ reverses the direction of dependence: God asks no provision from the household but provides it.
terra: The righteous servants inherit the earth, relocating inheritance from predatory seizure to the final outcome promised by God.
terra: The sacrificial provision is to be eaten and shared with ٱلْبَآئِسَ ٱلْفَقِيرَ, placing the afflicted poor at a communal meal.
terra: From the sacrificial animals, people are told to eat and feed both the contented and the one who asks, another table whose provision must circulate.
terra: The faithful qualities make their bearers the heirs, introducing an inheritance defined by character rather than accumulation.
terra: Those heirs inherit Firdaus and remain there, setting lasting inheritance against the perishable legacy people consume unjustly.

luna: Water is sent down in a measured amount and settled in the earth; it concretely joins provision, collected water, and the section's language of measure. | terra: Water descends بِقَدَرٍۢ and is lodged in the earth, uniting measure, gathered water, storage, and God's ability to remove it.
terra: The question asks whether the extension of wealth and sons is being mistaken for God hastening good things to its recipients.
terra: The answer is that they do not perceive, directly correcting the assumption that abundant provision itself certifies honor.
terra: People of wealth and abundance are forbidden to swear off giving kin, the needy, and emigrants, directly addressing the full vessel's temptation to close itself.
terra: Owners must give contracted dependents from the wealth God gave them, so divine gift creates a claim for release and liberation rather than permanent control.

luna: The Creator determines each created thing with precise measure, a direct parallel to the section's statement that everything has an amount and term. | terra: God creates every thing and determines it with exact determination, grounding all shares and limits in creation itself.

luna: The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but keep a course between; it supplies a boundary to the section's brim-full appetite for wealth. | terra: The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily but hold a just balance between them, a moral measure for the vessel.
terra: Pharaoh's people are removed from gardens and springs, beginning the transfer named as Israel's inheritance in 26:59.
terra: Treasures and an honorable station are added to what the departing people leave for others.
terra: وَأَوْرَثْنَٰهَا بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ names the recipients when Pharaoh's people leave gardens, springs, treasures, and honored dwellings.
terra: يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌۭ وَلَا بَنُونَ states the final boundary at which wealth and children provide no benefit.
terra: The she-camel has a drinking share and the people a drinking share on an appointed day, a concrete division of one water source into measured turns.

luna: This commands full measure and forbids diminishing what is due, a specific rule for not reducing another person's portion. | terra: أَوْفُوا۟ ٱلْكَيْلَ commands a full measure while forbidding those who cause loss, establishing the just boundary for the section's brimful measuring vessel.

luna: The following ayah commands weighing by a straight balance, completing the concrete measure of what people receive. | terra: وَزِنُوا۟ بِٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ adds the straight balance to the command for full measure.

luna: The next ayah forbids depriving people of their things and spreading corruption; it names the injustice that the fair measure in the preceding ayat prevents. | terra: Do not diminish people's things or spread corruption in the land; it connects unjust measure to the same corruption whose multiplication the section hears in 89:12.
terra: Those given double reward spend from what God provided them, linking received gift to outgoing support.
terra: Towns made insolent by livelihood become dwellings scarcely inhabited, and وَكُنَّا نَحْنُ ٱلْوَٰرِثِينَ joins lost sustenance, lost dwelling, and God's final inheritance.
terra: Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and lasting, separating a present share from permanent possession.

luna: Qarun's immense treasure is described as so abundant that its keys burden a strong group; this gives a concrete scene for wealth gathered beyond an ordinary share. | terra: Qarun's treasure-keys burden a strong company, and his people tell him not to exult; the full vessel has become physically and morally heavy.

luna: Qarun is told to seek the next life with what God gave him, do good, and not corrupt the land; it shows how large provision can be directed away from hoarding. | terra: Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter through what God gave, not forget his worldly share, do good, and not seek corruption; it sets apportioned use against hoarded, corrupting abundance.

luna: Qarun claims that his wealth came from knowledge he possessed; the answer that earlier generations stronger in power and wealth were destroyed confronts the section's mistaken reading of abundance as honor. | terra: Qarun attributes the wealth to knowledge he possesses, precisely the self-credit corrected when survivors recognize divine expansion and restriction in 28:82.
terra: Qarun comes out in adornment and people desiring worldly life wish for wealth like his, showing the social contagion of the competition for more.
terra: Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better, providing the interpretive boundary before Qarun and his store disappear.

luna: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, so neither accumulated wealth nor status protects him; this makes tangible the source section's claim that ownership returns and worldly holders disappear. | terra: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no faction or self-help can preserve the amassed abundance.
terra: After Qarun's collapse, those who desired his place recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the scene corrects the reading of abundant wealth as honor.
luna: Everything perishes except God, to whom judgment and return belong; this is another direct formulation of the inheritance passage's claim that possessions return to their enduring owner.
terra: People are told to seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks, locating the source of every share before its human holder.

luna: Creatures that do not carry their provision are still provided for by God, while humans are addressed too; this is a specific counterimage to gathering and storing as if stored wealth alone sustains life. | terra: Many creatures do not carry their provision; God provides them and people alike, loosening the imagined security of a personally stocked container.

luna: Allah expands and measures provision for His servants; in its context of created dependence, this repeats the section's claim that livelihood is allotted by God. | terra: ٱللَّهُ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ لَهُ repeats the apportioning formula and grounds it in God's knowledge of all things.

luna: The ayah asks whether people see God expanding provision for some and measuring it down for others, identifying these opposite conditions as signs rather than social verdicts. | terra: The question whether they see God expand and restrict provision makes changing allotment itself a sign, rather than proof of a person's worth.

luna: The relative, needy person, and traveler are each owed a حق; it states the distributive right of the poor in the vocabulary of the section's share and table. | terra: فَـَٔاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ again calls the portion given to relatives and the needy their due, not the owner's optional surplus.
terra: Usurious increase does not grow with God, whereas what is given as zakat seeking Him makes its givers the true multipliers; it reverses the section's worldly contest in increase.
terra: The promise to fill Hell with jinn and humans gives a fixed divine boundary to the otherwise insatiable image of 50:30.
terra: Those who leave their beds in fear and hope also spend from divine provision, pairing dependence on God with opening the vessel.
terra: Blood relatives are closer to one another in God's decree than other affiliations, another boundary preserving the proper recipients of a legacy.
terra: God causes the believers to inherit enemies' land, houses, and wealth, another collective transfer illustrating the section's basic w-r-th sense.
terra: A good dwelling with two gardens is called a sign, and its people are told to eat from their Lord's provision and thank Him.

luna: The wealthy say they have more wealth and children and therefore will not be punished; it is a direct example of mistaking abundance for divine favor, which the section rejects. | terra: The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, the precise false reading answered by divine expansion and restriction in 34:36.

luna: The formula that God expands and restricts provision appears against claims about wealth and children; the next ayah states that wealth and children do not themselves bring a person near to God. | terra: The answer to those boasting of greater wealth and children is that God expands and restricts provision, but most do not know what that abundance means.

luna: The response says wealth and children do not bring people near to God, while faith and good deeds do; it breaks the link between a large share and honor. | terra: Neither wealth nor children bring anyone near to God; faithful good action instead receives multiplied reward and secure dwellings.

luna: Whatever people spend is replaced by God, the best provider; this reverses the hoarder's belief that keeping a growing stock is what secures provision. | terra: After repeating expansion and restriction, the verse promises وَمَآ أَنفَقْتُم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ فَهُوَ يُخْلِفُهُۥ, turning divinely apportioned provision into confidence to spend.

luna: The revived earth produces حبًّا from which people eat; this uses the source section's secondary dictionary form حبّ for grain as actual food, the substance imagined in the needy person's filled jar. | terra: From dead earth God brings out حَبًّۭا فَمِنْهُ يَأْكُلُونَ, directly joining the section's grain-sense of h-b-b to eating.

terra: When told to spend from God's provision, disbelievers ask whether they should feed one whom God could feed; the objection directly dramatizes a community refusing to turn apportioned rizq into food.
terra: Solomon says he loved fine possessions over remembrance until they were hidden, a non-monetary instance of love filling attention and displacing what should govern it.
terra: إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَرِزْقُنَا مَا لَهُۥ مِن نَّفَادٍۢ describes divine provision as inexhaustible, unlike the finite stores people guard.
terra: لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكَ وَمِمَّن تَبِعَكَ closes the series of filling decrees and locates what the terrible vessel will contain.

luna: When prosperity comes, the person says it was obtained through his own knowledge, but the verse says it is a test; this directly challenges treating an expanded share as self-earned honor. | terra: After hardship, a person calls on God, then attributes the granted favor to personal knowledge; the verse calls it a trial, matching the section's correction of self-credit for provision.

luna: This asks whether people know God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it down, again denying that a person's share is self-made proof of worth. | terra: The verse again asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision, making the measure a sign against self-credit for wealth.
terra: The people of Paradise praise God for letting them inherit the land and settle wherever they wish, a lasting dwelling granted after worldly stores end.
terra: وَقَدَّرَ فِيهَآ أَقْوَٰتَهَا apportions the earth's sustenance in measured stages, equally for those who ask, uniting measure, food-support, and claimants.
terra: After adversity, a recipient of mercy says it is his and doubts the Hour, exposing how a granted share becomes a claim of permanent ownership.

luna: The verse says God expands and measures provision while holding the keys of heaven and earth, placing the measured share under divine command. | terra: God holds the keys of heaven and earth and expands or restricts provision, locating every human vessel inside His larger store and measure.

luna: It explains that unrestricted expansion to all servants would produce transgression, so provision is sent down in a measure; this gives a reason for the section's measured shares without calling poverty humiliation. | terra: If God expanded provision without limit people would transgress, so He sends it down بِقَدَرٍۢ مَّا يَشَآءُ; measured provision is presented as protection from the excess seen in the filled vessel.
terra: Whatever is given is merely enjoyment of the near life, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
terra: Those who answer their Lord conduct affairs by mutual consultation and spend from provision, a positive communal counterpart to failing to urge one another toward feeding.
terra: God sends water from heaven بِقَدَرٍۢ and revives dead land, making measured release rather than limitless filling the source of life.

luna: نحن قسمنا بينهم معيشتهم states that God apportioned people's livelihood among them; this is the section's central claim about who divides provision. | terra: نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ states that God, rather than the hoarder, apportions livelihoods; the q-s-m root joins the oath-word to the division of life's means.
terra: Paradise is declared the inheritance given because of deeds, reversing inheritance from an object of appetite into a moral outcome.
terra: Gardens and springs are the first possessions Pharaoh's people leave behind before another people inherit them in 44:28.
terra: Crops and noble dwellings add food and settled property to the estate that passes from one people to another.
terra: The comforts in which they delighted complete the inventory of a full life that does not remain with its holders.
terra: كَذَٰلِكَ وَأَوْرَثْنَٰهَا قَوْمًا ءَاخَرِينَ is the section's dictionary definition of inheritance staged historically: one people's goods become another people's possession.
terra: The tree of Zaqqum is introduced as the food awaiting the grave sinner, reversing food from support into punishment.
terra: طَعَامُ ٱلْأَثِيمِ explicitly names Zaqqum as the sinner's food.
terra: The food is like molten metal boiling in bellies, joining eating to an internal fire.
terra: Its boiling is compared with boiling scalding water, completing the transformation of the meal into flame-like torment.
terra: Disbelievers eat as cattle eat and the Fire is their lodging, placing unreflective consumption on a direct path to Hell.
terra: Were God to press people for all their wealth, they would become stingy and their resentments would emerge; the verse exposes the resistance named in 47:38.
terra: Those called to spend yet act stingily are stingy only against themselves; God is rich and they are poor, reversing the hoarder's estimate of who possesses and who needs.
terra: Blessed water descends and grows gardens and grain, supplying the water-mass and grain inside the section's imagined full jar from one divine source.
terra: Tall palms with clustered spathes add a visibly gathered, layered crop to the provision scene.
terra: رِّزْقًۭا لِّلْعِبَادِ names the rain-grown grain and fruit as provision for servants, rather than the accumulator's self-created stock.

luna: Hell is asked whether it is full and answers that it wants more; its unfillable appetite is the boundary opposite the source section's vessel filled to its brim. | terra: Hell is addressed as a vessel, هَلِ ٱمْتَلَأْتِ, and answers هَلْ مِن مَّزِيدٍۢ; it is the terrible, never-satisfied endpoint of the nearly overflowing wealth-container.

luna: Believers' wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived; that stated claim parallels the section's insistence that need is a claim on what others possess. | terra: وَفِىٓ أَمْوَٰلِهِمْ حَقٌّۭ لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ places a due share for the asker and deprived inside the owner's wealth, exactly the portion the section says must leave the vessel.
terra: وَفِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ رِزْقُكُمْ locates people's provision beyond the vessel they presently control, reinforcing that its source and promised measure are not theirs.
terra: God seeks no provision from people and does not ask them to feed Him, reversing any idea that the Provider depends on the stocked vessel.
terra: God alone is the Provider and possessor of firm power, grounding all human provision and feeding in His sufficiency.

luna: The Qur'an calls the pagans' allocation of daughters to God and sons to themselves an unjust division, giving ق س م a specific contrary boundary to fair shares. | terra: The condemned assignment is called قِسْمَةٌۭ ضِيزَىٰ, an unjust division, supplying a direct Quranic judgment on corrupted apportionment.
terra: The she-camel trial declares that water is قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ and each drinking turn is attended, a concrete instance of one gathered resource becoming scheduled shares.

luna: إنا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر gives the section's claim that everything has a measure a direct Qur'anic formulation. | terra: إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَٰهُ بِقَدَرٍۢ gives the section's universal claim that every thing has a measure its concise Quranic formulation.
terra: God sets the balance after raising heaven, placing human measures under a larger created order.
terra: أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا۟ فِى ٱلْمِيزَانِ forbids excess in the balance, the boundary violated by taking more than one's share.
terra: Establish weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient; both overfilling oneself and underfilling another are corrected.
terra: The earth holds grain with husks among its provisions, another direct occurrence of the h-b-b grain sense.
luna: Everything on earth perishes, matching the section's claim that all besides God passes away and possessions do not remain with their present owners.
luna: The next ayah says the face of the Lord remains; it supplies the enduring side of the source section's contrast between what vanishes and the true owner.
terra: The astray are told they will eat from the tree of Zaqqum, turning voracious worldly eating into a punitive meal.
terra: They will fill their bellies from Zaqqum, a bodily container filled with the opposite of sustaining provision.
terra: They then drink scalding water over the hellish food, continuing the reversed table.
terra: Their drinking is like desperately thirsty camels, so even a filled belly produces no sufficiency.

luna: Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the wealth is held in trust, which reverses the section's claim of absolute possession. | terra: The command to spend from what God has made people successors over treats present possession as a temporary stewardship, directly joining spending to the section's claim about ultimate inheritance.

luna: The inheritance of the heavens and earth belongs to God, and the verse urges spending before that return; this directly links present wealth to the source section's final-owner claim. | terra: The question why people do not spend is grounded in وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَٰثُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ, so divine inheritance turns the section's claim about ultimate ownership into a demand to release wealth now.
terra: The one who lends God a good loan has it multiplied and receives a generous reward, making released wealth the source of lasting increase.
terra: Charitable men and women who lend God well have their gift multiplied, another explicit reversal of increase through retention.

luna: This ayah names boasting and competition in wealth and children, then compares worldly life to crops that grow, yellow, and become debris; it joins multiplication, provision, and what passes away. | terra: Worldly life includes boasting and تَكَاثُرٌۭ فِى ٱلْأَمْوَٰلِ, then becomes dry debris like rain-grown plants, making the contest in increase visibly perishable.
terra: Feeding sixty needy people is the required expiation for one unable to perform the preceding remedies, another legal scene in which food becomes the needy person's due.

luna: The distribution of captured wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers is expressly intended to keep it from circulating only among the rich; this sharpens the section's concern with who gets a share. | terra: Fay is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler كَىْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةًۢ بَيْنَ ٱلْأَغْنِيَآءِ, an explicit rule against wealth circulating only at the rich end of the table.
terra: Poor emigrants driven from homes and property seek God's bounty, making material deprivation a loss of dwelling and livelihood rather than mere lack of coins.
terra: The hosts prefer others over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌۭ, even in need, and are saved from avarice; their vessel opens despite its own shortfall.
terra: Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembrance, matching the distraction named by ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ while marking its remedy.
terra: Spend from provision before death, when the withholder will ask for delay to give charity; the sealed vessel is opened only too late.

luna: The verse calls wealth and children a trial, matching the section's account of being tested through expanded or restricted provision rather than thereby honored or abased. | terra: إِنَّمَآ أَمْوَٰلُكُمْ وَأَوْلَٰدُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ identifies wealth as a trial, supporting the section's correction of the claim that expanded or restricted provision proves honor or humiliation.
terra: The command to spend and the promise of success for one protected from inner stinginess show how the wealth-trial in 64:15 is passed.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so the portion leaving one's hand is not the portion finally lost.

luna: After promising provision from unexpected sources and sufficiency for the trusting person, the verse says God has set a measure for everything, echoing the section's q-d-r gloss. | terra: قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدْرًۭا states almost verbatim the section's dictionary premise that every thing has a measure.
terra: مَن قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقُهُ closely repeats 89:16, but commands the person under that constraint to spend from what God gave and promises ease after hardship.
terra: The question who could provide if God withheld His provision exposes every stored share as dependent on continued divine giving.
terra: The owners of the garden swear to harvest it in the morning, opening a scene of abundant food treated as exclusively theirs.
terra: They make no exception, showing confidence that the crop and its measure are fully under their control.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, beginning the loss that answers their plan to reserve every share.
terra: The fertile garden becomes كَٱلصَّرِيمِ overnight, an emptied field answering the owners' determination to keep its full yield from the needy.
terra: They set out early to cut the crop, moving toward the act that would fill their own containers.
terra: أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌۭ is the garden owners' whispered plan to exclude every needy person from the harvest.
terra: They go out عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍۢ قَٰدِرِينَ with determined confidence in their power, while the garden has already been emptied beyond their knowledge.
terra: On seeing the ruined garden, the owners first think they have lost their way, showing how completely expected abundance has vanished.
terra: بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ makes the would-be deprivers recognize themselves as the deprived after the crop is taken away.
terra: Their most balanced member asks why they did not glorify God, identifying forgotten divine ownership inside the failed harvest plan.
terra: The owners glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, the first truthful response after trying to exclude the needy.
terra: They turn on one another in blame, exposing the failed communal counsel behind their shared plan to withhold the crop.
terra: The owners confess إِنَّا كُنَّا طَٰغِينَ, naming exclusion of the needy from abundance as transgression.
terra: After losing the crop, they hope their Lord will exchange it for a better garden, turning ownership back into dependence on divine allotment.
terra: كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْعَذَابُ makes the emptied garden an anticipatory judgment and points beyond it to the greater final punishment.
terra: أُوتِىَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِشِمَالِهِ identifies the left-hand recipient whose useless wealth, chaining, and failure to urge feeding unfold in 69:28-37.

luna: The left-handed person asks what his wealth has availed him; this answers the source section's image of love and accumulation with wealth's failure at judgment. | terra: The left-hand recipient's مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ declares the final uselessness of the wealth whose gathering displaced the needy; 69:25 identifies the speaker.
terra: The left-hand recipient says his authority has perished after saying wealth did not avail, so both stored property and the power built around it collapse.
terra: خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ begins the chaining whose causes are separately named in 69:33-34, giving the section's claimed consequence its own action.
terra: ثُمَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ moves the one who withheld food and gathered wealth into the fire, completing the devouring-to-fire trajectory.
terra: The command to thread him through a seventy-cubit chain specifies the binding that the section says follows the refused urging of needy-food.

luna: This ayah says the left-handed person did not believe in God the Great; the following 69:34 separately names the failure to urge feeding the needy, so the moral and social claims stay distinct. | terra: Failure to believe in God is named as the first cause beside failure to urge feeding in 69:34, preserving the passage's two stated grounds rather than making food the sole cause.

luna: The person handed the book in his left hand is condemned for not urging طعام المسكين; this gives the same refusal the section cites as a reason for judgment. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ is the same refused urging, now named as a cause of the left-hand recipient's punishment.
terra: وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ reverses the withheld table: the one who did not urge feeding now has no food except foul discharge.
terra: لَّا يَأْكُلُهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱلْخَٰطِـُٔونَ identifies the sinners as eaters of that hellish food, closing the reversal begun by eating others' shares.
terra: The fire following the stower's refusal is لَظَىٰ, introducing the consuming answer to gathering and putting away in 70:18.

luna: The Fire calls the one who turned away, before the next ayah identifies the one who gathered and stored; this completes the section's movement from hoarding the vulnerable's share to judgment. | terra: The blaze تَدْعُوا۟ مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ calls the person who turned away before 70:18 names his gathering and storage.

luna: وجمع فأوعى describes gathering and putting away in a container, closely matching both the source section's root لمم for gathering all and its bowl image. | terra: وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰٓ shows the same two motions as the section's image: gathering and putting the result into a containing vessel.
terra: Humanity is described as anxiously grasping, introducing the response to good and harm that explains the gatherer and stower later in the passage.
terra: When harm touches the anxious person, he becomes impatient, one side of the insecurity that accumulation tries to master.

luna: When good reaches a person, this ayah says he becomes withholding; it names the response to abundance that the section condemns in the wealthy who will not feed the needy. | terra: When good touches him, he becomes withholding, the exact inward motion that closes provision against other claimants.

luna: The righteous are described as having a known right in their wealth, corresponding to the section's account of provision as an allotted share rather than unbounded private ownership. | terra: The prayerful have حَقٌّۭ مَّعْلُومٌۭ in their wealth, a known and measured share opposed to indiscriminate accumulation.

luna: This ayah names the asker and deprived as the recipients of that known right, specifying the needy whom the section's hoarder ignores. | terra: لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ names the requester and deprived as owners of the known share in 70:24.
terra: Noah describes people following leaders whose wealth and children increase them only in loss, reversing abundance from success into ruin.
terra: The condemned man is reminded that God gave him extensive wealth, locating the filled store as a gift rather than self-made possession.
terra: ثُمَّ يَطْمَعُ أَنْ أَزِيدَ shows the recipient of extensive wealth still craving that God add more, the full vessel's unsatisfied appetite.
terra: The answer كَلَّآ sets a firm refusal against his demand for still more.
terra: The people of the right ask the offenders what brought them into Saqar, introducing the confession that includes failure to feed the needy.
terra: The offenders first confess that they were not among those who prayed, preserving the co-cause stated beside refusal to feed in 74:44.

luna: Those in the Fire say they were not among those who fed the needy, another explicit account of refusing the food given to the miskin. | terra: وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ is the condemned speakers' own admission that they did not feed the needy, one stated cause of entering Saqar.

luna: They give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite حبّه; the same love that fills the rich person's appetite is emptied into food for people who need it. | terra: وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ gives beloved food to the needy, orphan, and captive; the same love that fills 89's vessel here empties it into other mouths.
terra: The feeders say they feed only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, showing how the beloved food is released without creating a new claim over its recipients.
luna: The cups in the Garden are set to a precise measure, قَدَّرُوهَا تَقْدِيرًا; this is a measured cup in contrast to the section's imagined vessel filled to excess.
terra: Rain is sent so that grain and vegetation may be brought forth, joining the secondary grain sense to divine supply.
terra: فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِۦ asks the human to look at the origin of his food before the passage names the grain.
terra: فَأَنۢبَتْنَا فِيهَا حَبًّۭا gives the Quranic grain-sense of h-b-b cited by the section and locates the desired food in God's growth from earth.
terra: مَّتَٰعًۭا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَٰمِكُمْ names the whole food-producing sequence as provision for people and their animals.

luna: This ayah warns the measure-cheaters; 83:2–3 specify that they take full measure for themselves and give others less, completing the row's own warning with a concrete parallel to swallowing another's share. | terra: وَيْلٌۭ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ condemns those who manipulate the measure, the commercial form of taking more than one's apportioned share.

luna: Those who measure for themselves take the full amount, the self-favoring half of a trading-scale case that illuminates the section's undivided taking of an estate. | terra: When they take measure from people, يَسْتَوْفُونَ, they demand it in full, showing the vessel filled at the powerful person's end.

luna: When measuring or weighing for others, they give less; although this is trade rather than inheritance, it is a precise reversal of fair shares and echoes taking the whole inheritance. | terra: When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish, making the needy end of the same transaction underfilled.
terra: The short-measurers are asked whether they expect to be resurrected, making final accountability the reason a commercial measure cannot be manipulated.
terra: The resurrection is for a tremendous day, locating the apparently small theft from another's measure inside judgment.
terra: People will stand before the Lord of the worlds, the endpoint at which every underfilled share is answered.
terra: The humbled have no food except a bitter thorn, a punitive counterpart to the sustaining food withheld from the needy.
terra: That food neither nourishes nor removes hunger, exactly negating the section's idea that provision enables a weak person to remain.
terra: فَلَا ٱقْتَحَمَ ٱلْعَقَبَةَ frames the feeding acts of 90:14-16 as the difficult moral ascent the hoarder has declined.
terra: فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍۢ places freeing a person alongside hungry-day feeding, widening the steep path from food to release of the vulnerable.

luna: The steep ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, matching the section's concrete act of giving food when need is sharp. | terra: أَوْ إِطْعَٰمٌۭ فِى يَوْمٍۢ ذِى مَسْغَبَةٍۢ makes feeding on a day of hunger the concrete crossing of the steep path.

luna: The hungry recipient may be a nearby orphan, extending the section's paired concern with inheritance and the meal of the needy. | terra: يَتِيمًۭا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ identifies the near orphan as one recipient of the feeding in 90:14, joining kinship and orphanhood at the table.

luna: The other recipient is a poor person in the dust, a concrete image of the weak person whose food the section says is withheld. | terra: أَوْ مِسْكِينًۭا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍۢ identifies the other recipient as a needy person brought down to the dust, making the section's dictionary sense of weakness visible.

luna: After the meal in hunger, this ayah describes believers urging one another to patience and compassion; it completes the communal mutual-encouragement dimension without claiming it repeats the food command. | terra: Mutual counsel to patience and mercy gives a positive communal counterpart to the reciprocal urging abandoned in 89:18.

luna: This ayah identifies the people who counsel patience and compassion after the feeding and mutual exhortation in 90:14–17 as companions of the right; it completes the social outcome while its own contribution is that classification.

luna: The one who gives and is mindful of God is promised ease; it is a specific opposite to the section's refusal to direct wealth toward the needy. | terra: فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَٱتَّقَىٰ begins the opposite type from the self-sufficient miser: the person who gives and remains mindful.
terra: Believing in the best promise gives the giver's release of wealth its inward ground.

luna: The next ayah says God will facilitate the giver's ease, linking giving to a provision that does not need to be secured by hoarding. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises ease to the giver, reversing the instinct that safety comes from keeping the vessel full.

luna: The person who is miserly, self-sufficient, and denies the best promise forms the explicit opposite of the giver in the preceding passage and matches the section's rich refusal. | terra: The person who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient embodies the closed, full vessel.
terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ answers the withholder's imagined security with a course toward hardship.

luna: The miser's wealth will not avail him when he falls; it completes the section's warning that accumulated possessions do not protect at judgment. | terra: وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُۥ مَالُهُۥٓ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ repeats the left-hand recipient's discovery that amassed wealth cannot avail at the fall.
terra: فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ forbids overpowering the orphan, the vulnerable heir standing beside the needy in the section.
terra: وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids repelling the requester, making visible the person who asks the full vessel for food.
luna: The human transgresses when seeing himself as self-sufficient; this describes the stance that permits the section's wealthy person to ignore the needy.
luna: The following ayah says the self-sufficient one crosses bounds, completing the preceding trigger of imagined independence from provision.

luna: After describing the person who transgresses upon feeling self-sufficient, this ayah says the return is to his Lord; it completes the section's link between imagined independence through wealth and final return.

luna: The human is described as intense in love of wealth, a direct parallel to the section's حبًّا جمًّا. | terra: وَإِنَّهُۥ لِحُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ is the Quran's other concentrated portrait of intense love of wealth, directly echoing حُبًّا جَمًّا.

luna: The competition in accumulating more distracts people, a direct Qur'anic occurrence of the source's k-th-r idea of rivalry in wealth and status. | terra: أَلْهَىٰكُمُ ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ names the rivalry in increase that the section hears in the old sense of 89:12's multiplying verb.

luna: The next ayah says this distraction lasts until the graves are visited; it completes the preceding competition's endpoint and shows wealth cannot extend life. | terra: حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ ٱلْمَقَابِرَ gives the contest for more its limit in the grave, where no filled store remains usable.
terra: لَتَرَوُنَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ shows the fire at the end of the rivalry for increase announced in 102:1.
terra: ثُمَّ لَتُسْـَٔلُنَّ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَنِ ٱلنَّعِيمِ turns enjoyed abundance into a questioned trust rather than proof of honor.

luna: The one who gathers wealth and counts it is the exact collector named by the section's image of gathering the whole inheritance. | terra: ٱلَّذِى جَمَعَ مَالًۭا وَعَدَّدَهُۥ stages the section's full vessel as a person gathering wealth and repeatedly counting it.

luna: This collector thinks his wealth makes him immortal, the precise false security that the section places beside the overflowing store. | terra: The collector يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُۥ mistakes accumulated wealth for permanence, exposing the hope hidden inside the filled jar.

luna: Immediately after the collector who thinks wealth makes him immortal, this ayah says he will be thrown into the Crusher; it completes the source section's link between accumulated wealth and fire. | terra: The wealth-counter is hurled into ٱلْحُطَمَةِ, so the container he filled does not preserve him but leads to crushing destruction.
terra: نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ identifies the Crusher as God's kindled fire, completing the section's turn from gathered wealth to consuming flame.

luna: This asks about the denier of judgment; the linked 107:2–3 specifies the orphan-shoving and failure to urge feeding that the section treats as that person's portrait. | terra: The question who denies the Judgment identifies the stance embodied by repelling the orphan and refusing to urge needy-food in the next two ayat.

luna: The one who denies judgment is shown shoving the orphan away; this supplies the vulnerable person excluded from the section's table. | terra: فَذَٰلِكَ ٱلَّذِى يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ supplies the orphan-repelling act paired with refusal to urge needy-food in 107:3.

luna: ولا يحض على طعام المسكين directly says he does not urge feeding the needy, matching the section's reciprocal failure to encourage feeding. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats the section's failure to urge feeding the needy; its singular verb also clarifies what the reciprocal plural in 89:18 makes a communal failure.
terra: The closing charge that they withhold small acts of aid extends the closed table from food to ordinary useful things neighbors need.

luna: Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings avail him nothing; this is a direct limit on the security the source section's hoarder expects from possessions. | terra: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ repeats the verdict that wealth and acquisition do not avail their owner.
terra: سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًۭا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍۢ places the owner whose wealth does not avail directly into flame.
